Selective in-mold bonding 4DT IM
PP 579S and Haitian ZE1200 IM machine were utilized for selective in-mold bonding 4D IM. Experimental molds wAith three cavity structures—designed for cross-shaped, hand-shaped, and caterpillar-shaped parts—were employed (Fig. 3a).
A hot compaction machine (TY-7006, Jiangsu Tianyuan Experimental Equipment Co., Ltd) was used to fabricate PP sheets measuring 100 × 60 × 0.4 mm3. PP pellets were compacted at 180 °C and 6 MPa for 5 minutes. The prepared sheets were cut to the required dimensions for in-mold bonding. The small component piece was positioned at selected bonding locations in the mold and temporarily fixed using double-sided tape. During IM, the polymer melt encapsulated the piece, and the high melt temperature softened its surface, enabling fusion and solidification with the surrounding matrix. After demolding, residual adhesive on the part surface was removed with ethyl alcohol.
Numerical simulations of the IM process for the cross-shaped part were conducted using Moldex3D. The cross-shaped part geometry was modeled, and the total mesh comprised 337,197 elements, including 125,595 for the part, 17,645 for the runner, 70,869 for the insert, and 123,088 for the mold. The p was maintained at 35 MPa, and the mold temperature (T ) was set to 25 inj mold °C. The initial process conditions of T = 250 °C, p = 24 MPa, t = 4 s, and t = 13 s were melt pack pack cool initially used to analyze the IM process and warpage deformation of the root-position bonded part (Bond 1, Fig. 3b). A comparative analysis of three bonding positions (Bond 1–3) was subsequently conducted under identical process conditions: T = 220 °C, p = 18 MPa, t = 4 s, and t = melt pack pack cool 13 s (Supplementary Fig. 7a–e, Supplementary Movie 2, Supplementary Note 2). Experimental validation parts (Supplementary Fig. 7b) were fabricated using the Haitian ZE1200 IM machine under the same process parameters as the simulations. Part deformations were qualified in the Z-direction displacements using the HG-C100 laser displacement sensor with the measurement platform, relative to the pre-marked datum and measurement points on the parts (Supplementary Fig. 1b). A very strong linear correlation was observed between the simulated and experimental warpage displacements (R2 = 99.79%, Pearson r = 0.9989)49 (Supplementary Fig. 7d).
The T , p , t , and t were varied according to the RSM-designed conditions melt pack pack cool (Supplementary Table 12) to analyze their effects on the warpage deformation of the cross-shaped parts with Bond 1 (Supplementary Fig. 7f,g). The effect of p was most significant, followed by pack T . The influence of other single factors is insignificant. Higher T resulted in stronger melt melt interfacial bonding, leading to reduced warpage. Increasing p improved melt compensation and pack enhanced material consolidation at the bonding interface, which lowered shrinkage gradients and reduced warpage. However, at higher p (35 MPa), the melt became over-compressed, creating pack larger thermal gradients and higher frozen-in residual stresses, especially near the bonding interface, which increased warpage after demolding. The minimum in the curve therefore reflects the balance between these two competing effects. Increasing t and t slightly reduced pack cool displacement.
The local interfacial strength of the cross-shaped part was assessed using a nanoindenter (G200, KLA Corporation) in compliance with ISO 14577. To meet the equipment's size requirements, the bonded portion of the part was cut into samples measuring 14 × 10 × 1 mm3. The embedded part's surface area was tested in load-displaceme nt mode, with a maximum displacement of 2.5 μm, a holding time of 20 s, and a loading speed of 10 nm s-1. Seven test points were randomly measured on each of the three samples (Bond 1–3). The load-displacement curves (Supplementary Fig. 8a) at Bond 1 for different test points show significant deviations, indicating sensitivity to T and p changes and residual stress. In contrast, Bonds 2 and 3 exhibited smaller deviations, indicating more uniform bonding. Elastic modulus and hardness were highest for Bond 2, while Bond 1 showed significant deviations, and Bond 3 demonstrated moderate and stable values (Supplementary Fig. 8b). The modulus distribution of Bond 3 was most uniform, slightly lower than Bond 2, and higher than Bond 1 in several results, indicating sufficient bonding from effective melting and resolidification despite its distance from the gate (Supplementary Fig. 8c).

RSM modeling for programmable part shapes of selective in-molding bonding 4D IM
The Box-Behnken design within the RSM framework was employed, following the six-stage modeling procedure outlined (Supplementary Fig. 6a). The bonding position was defined as the variable I. Three bonding positions (Bond 1, 2, and 3) were defined along one blade of the cross-shaped part, spanning from the root to the edge (Fig. 3a). ## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The paper addresses the traditional challenge in injection molding (IM) where non-uniform material shrinkage leads to undesirable warpage and dimensional deviations in plastic parts. Instead of minimizing warpage, the authors propose to leverage and control this shrinkage to induce purposeful, programmable deformation, enabling the creation of complex, customized geometries from a single mold.
The core contribution is the proposal and demonstration of 4D Injection Molding (4D IM). Two techniques were used to demonstrate these: Localized Thermal Activation 4D IM and Selective In-Mold Bonding 4D IM. Then, the application on composites and elastomers was performed.
I suggest that the authors address the following comments:
The paper should be better divided so that the reader can easily follow the research's progression.
The introduction should provide the necessary background and context, explaining more precisely what was done before regarding this issue.
The figures (1-2-3) are pretty dense with information, and the labels/text within the images can be small, making them challenging to decipher without significant zooming. Consider increasing font sizes for labels and legends within the figures, or providing higher-resolution images. If possible, simplify some of the more complex diagrams or break them into multiple sub-figures for better clarity. Ensure units are clearly visible and consistently labeled in all figures and graphs.
The section "Methods" provides details; some of the experimental specifics could be briefly introduced earlier when the concept is first discussed to give a clearer picture of the practical implementation.
The paper extensively references "4D printing" and "additive manufacturing" techniques, highlighting their limitations in mass production. While 4D IM is presented as a solution, a more direct comparison or quantitative analysis of the scalability and cost-efficiency benefits of 4D IM over existing 4D printing methods would strengthen the argument. Please include a more direct, quantitative comparison (e.g., production rate, cost per part, material waste) with existing 4D printing or additive manufacturing techniques that aim for similar customized geometries. This would highlight the "mass production" advantage of 4D IM.
The statement "The injection filling time was 0.19 s (Extended Data Fig. 1b)" (line 294) seems relatively short for an IM process, even for small parts. While simulations might handle this, a brief comment on the implications of such a rapid filling time or its practical feasibility for larger or more complex parts would be beneficial.
While the R² values for RSM models are high, some predicted R² values for composites (e.g., 54.37% for failure strain, line 520) are relatively low. Although the authors state "acceptable accuracy," a more in-depth discussion on the reasons for these lower accuracies, the potential contributing factors (e.g., material variability, complexity of fiber-matrix interaction, measurement challenges), and potential ways to improve them would be valuable.
A deeper insight into "Limitations" would be beneficial in explicitly stating the current constraints or challenges of 4D IM (e.g., complexity of mold design for heating elements, potential for bond displacement under extreme conditions, and the need for further material characterization) even if some are mentioned in the discussion.
Future work could be expanded beyond general applications to specific research directions and applications.

Ensure consistent use of LaTeX for all Δ symbols.

### Reviewer 3

The paper presents an advanced 4D Injection Moulding (4D IM) platform capable of programmable deformations, selective in-mould bonding for multi-material and multi-functional structures, and integration of functional elements such as embedded magnets for soft robotics.
While the work demonstrates significant innovation, some improvements should be made to increase the final quality of the paper to be completely ready for submission.
A general remark: the Conclusion section is missing, together with Future works.
More in detail, but also as a suggestion for Future works, there were areas where it was not possible to integrate more of the work done, with the purpose of moving the 4D IM platform from a laboratory-scale proof-of-concept toward a robust, industrially viable manufacturing technology:
The feasibility of scaling the localised heating system and multi-point bonding for high-volume production remains unclear.
The complexity and cost associated with multiple heating elements and precise voltage control may limit adoption in large-scale manufacturing.
Although experimental correlations are generally strong, some parts, such as the caterpillar-shaped samples, show lower predictive accuracy (R² = 81.57%), indicating variability. Data on repeated production cycles, mould wear, and long-term stability are currently lacking.
In TPU/Fe₃O₄ composites, particle aggregation at higher loadings reduces magnetic field uniformity, which may compromise actuation performance. Long-term mechanical behavior, including fatigue and multi-cycle performance, has not been fully investigated.
Demonstrations of soft robotic functionalities have been limited to controlled laboratory conditions. The performance under practical operating conditions, including higher loads, integration with industrial automation, and electronic systems, has not yet been validated.
The current studies provide limited insight into compliance with ISO or other industrial production and quality standards.
Durability testing, functional certification, and standardization data are largely absent.

Response: We have revised all figures to enhance clarity. This includes increasing font sizes for some labels and legends, break complex diagrams into multiple sub-figures for better clarity, and ensuring all units are consistently and clearly visible. We have definitely provided high-resolution versions of all figures upon submission of the revised manuscript.
Comment 4: The section "Methods" provides details; some of the experimental specifics could be briefly introduced earlier when the concept is first discussed to give a clearer picture of the practical implementation.
Response: As suggested, we have integrated key methodological details (e.g., material types, brief descriptions of the molding and activation setups) into the main text when the concepts are first introduced, providing a clearer picture for the reader without delving into excessive detail upfront.
Comment 5: The paper extensively references "4D printing" and "additive manufacturing" techniques, highlighting their limitations in mass production. While 4D IM is presented as a solution, a more direct comparison or quantitative analysis of the scalability and cost-efficiency benefits of 4D IM over existing 4D printing methods would strengthen the argument. Please include a more direct, quantitative comparison (e.g., production rate, cost per part, material waste) with existing 4D printing or additive manufacturing techniques that aim for similar customized geometries. This would highlight the "mass production" advantage of 4D IM.
Response: Thank you for this valuable feedback. We have substantially strengthened the manuscript by adding a direct, quantitative comparison of the scalability and cost-efficiency of 4D IM relative to regular IM, existing 3D and 4D printing. Specifically, we have added a new paragraph in the Introduction section that provides a direct comparison. Further, we have added a comparison Table (Supplementary Table 25) and a new subsection in the Results (“Quantitative comparison of scalability”) that provides side-by-side numerical benchmarks for production rate, cycle time, cost per part, tooling cost, dimensional tolerance, and material waste across 4D IM, conventional IM, AM, and 4D printing. The relative References have also been given. These additions quantitatively highlight the mass-production advantages of 4D IM, showing that it uniquely combines the scalability of injection molding with the geometric programmability of 4D functional transformation, whereas existing 4D printing methods remain limited by low throughput, high per-part cost, and significant material inefficiency.
Comment 6: The statement "The injection filling time was 0.19 s (Extended Data Fig. 1b)" (line 294) seems relatively short for an IM process, even for small parts. While simulations might handle this, a brief comment on the implications of such a rapid filling time or its practical feasibility for larger or more complex parts would be beneficial.
Response: We have added a comment in the Methods section acknowledging this filling time: “The injection filling time of 0.19 s (Supplementary Fig. 2b), agrees well with the theoretical value derived from the specified injection speed (15 mm/s), cavity volume (2.28 cm3), and screw diameter (32 mm).” The theoretical filling time is calculated as: 2.28/(15*π*32*32/4)=0.189 s. The IM machine (Haitian ZE1200, 32-mm screw diameter, 170-mm stroke) provides a maximum shot volume of 136 cm³, which is significantly larger than the required melt volume (2.28 cm3). The short filling time results from the small cavity volume and is consistent with operating conditions commonly observed in high-speed injection molding (HSIM). Such rapid filling is well within the practical range of HSIM, a widely used industrial process characterized by extremely short filling times (0.05–0.25 s), high injection rates, and thin-wall geometries. For larger parts, the fill time would scale accordingly, and process windows (including filling time) would need to be re-optimized, which is a standard practice in IM.
Comment 7: While the R² values for RSM models are high, some predicted R² values for composites (e.g., 54.37% for failure strain, line 520) are relatively low. Although the authors state "acceptable accuracy," a more in-depth discussion on the reasons for these lower accuracies, the potential contributing factors (e.g., material variability, complexity of fiber-matrix interaction, measurement challenges), and potential ways to improve them would be valuable.
Response: We agree that, although most models exhibit high predictive performance, the predicted R² for failure strain (54.37%) is relatively lower. We have added the Pearson correlation coefficient (r) and the relative interpretation criteria [Ref. 49] for a further demonstration in the Result section and the Method section:
“The developed models (Eqs. 7–10) exhibited solid predictive performance (R2 = 79.5%, 68.09%, 99.21%, and 54.37% for warpage, strength, modulus, and failure stain) and strong linear relationships [49], as indicated by the Pearson correlation coefficient (r = 0.892, 0.825, 0.996, and 0.737) (Supplementary Tables 22,23).”
“The corresponding Pearson r values were 0.892, 0.825, 0.996, and 0.737, indicating strong (≥0.7) and very strong (≥0.9) linear relationships [49].”
Further, we have added a more detailed discussion in Supplementary Note 3 section to clarify the underlying reasons and potential improvements. The relatively lower predicted R² for failure strain is likely due to the complex, stochastic nature of fiber-matrix interactions and potential local variations in fiber orientation, which are challenging to capture perfectly with a phenomenological model. We suggest that future work could incorporate more direct microstructural metrics and integrate interation terms or hybrid machine-learning-assisted matamodels to improve predictive accuracy.
Comment 8: A deeper insight into "Limitations" would be beneficial in explicitly stating the current constraints or challenges of 4D IM (e.g., complexity of mold design for heating elements, potential for bond displacement under extreme conditions, and the need for further material characterization) even if some are mentioned in the discussion.
Response: We have substantially expanded the “Discussion” section to explicitly articulate the current limitations of the 4D IM platform. The revised section now provides deeper insights into several key constraints:
(1) the dependence of programmable deformation magnitude and spatial resolution on part geometry (e.g., reduced shape-change capability in thicker regions),
(2) the increased mold design complexity and energy demand associated with implementing localized thermal activation through integrated heating systems,
(3) the sensitivity of the selective bonding step to adhesive application quality, including potential variability in bond strength and surface artifacts,
(4) material-related challenges for composite and elastomer systems, where microstructural heterogeneity may reduce deformation predictability.
Additionally, we now highlight future directions targeting these constraints, such as non-contact thermal activation approaches (e.g., directed infrared heating), improved temporary adhesive strategies to ensure reliable yet removable bonding, and the integration of microstructural descriptors or hybrid machine-learning-assisted metamodels for enhanced deformation robustness.
Comment 9: Future work could be expanded beyond general applications to specific research directions and applications.
Response: We have revised the "Discussion" section to outline specific, actionable research directions for the "Future Work”:
“Future developments of the 4D IM framework will target these limitations. One direction is the adoption of non-contact thermal activation methods (e.g., directed infrared heating [60]) to generate spatial T gradients without permanent mold modification, thereby improving flexibility, energy efficiency, and cost-effectiveness. Another is the exploration of alternative bonding strategies, such as temporary high-performance adhesives [61] that form mechanical interlock interfaces between the bond part and cavity surface during molding and can be removed afterward to preserve surface quality. For composites and elastomers, greater material variability and more complex fiber/filler–matrix interactions may reduce model robustness for programmable deformation. Future studies will incorporate additional microstructural descriptors and hybrid machine-learning-assisted metamodels to enhance predictive accuracy and reliability. Performance validation under realistic operating conditions, including higher loads, multi-cycle actuation, and integration with automated or electronic systems, will also be required. Moreover, systematic evaluation of long-term durability, functional certification, and compliance with industrial standards will be essential for transitioning 4D IM from controlled laboratory demonstrations to robust industrial deployment.”
We also specify potential application domains where these advancements could have the highest impact, including deployable consumer products, morphing wearable devices, adaptive automotive/aerospace components, and stimuli-responsive structural parts in robotics.

Response: Thank you for catching this. The typo has been corrected, and we have ensured all Δ symbols are consistently formatted throughout the manuscript and supplementary information.

Comment 2. L63: Few recent papers on warpage control in AM should be cited.

However, warpage-control strategies in AM were not previously discussed in detail because the objective of this manuscript is to translate the deformation mechanisms established in 4D printing into a 4D IM framework. Accordingly, our emphasis has been placed on deformation mechanisms and functional applications rather than AM-specific warpage control. Comment 3. L133: The authors have used both DoE using OA and RSM. Can they specify why not just one is used throughout?

In our study, the Orthogonal Array (OA) design was used only for the localized thermal activation method, where the aim was to efficiently screen five injection molding parameters and identify the few factors with statistically significant effects on warpage (Supplementary Fig. 3g (originally Extended Data Fig. 1g)). This allowed us to determine optimized processing conditions before conducting the subsequent heating-element modeling.
The RSM models were built exclusively for the local heating parameters, where eight groups of heating elements served as the input factors while the injection molding parameters were fixed. We intentionally avoided mixing molding parameters with local heating parameters in a single model to reduce model complexity and prevent compounding uncertainties. A model focused solely on heating parameters provides more stable predictions and a more direct basis for control implementation.
For the selective in-mold bonding method, only RSM was employed. This value is determined primarily by the thickness ratio between the bonded CGF-PA6 prepreg tape (0.3 mm) and the mold cavity (2.0 mm), which results in a mold-to-bond thickness ratio of 6.7:1. The total mesh comprised 1,495,229 elements, including 212,037 for the part, 10,471 for the cold runner, and 1,272,721 for the mold. Comment 11. Fig. 2b: Why is the total Z-displacement smaller than the out-of-plane one? It seems counterintuitive. Same with Fig. 3b.
Response: The seemingly counterintuitive result arises from the fact that the two shrinkage components, Δv and Δv , act in different directions and partially offset each other. Before ejection, Δv develops while the melt is still hot and confined in the mold. Under high pressure and strong mold constraint, this shrinkage occurs mainly in-plane, and its Z-component is relatively small. The direction of the Δv -induced deformation is governed by the pressure and temperature gradients across the thickness, causing the blade to deform slightly along the Z-direction opposite to the gate. After ejection, Δv becomes dominant. This out-of-plane deformation is driven primarily by through-thickness thermal gradients (ΔT=T - T ). The part deflects toward the hotter region—near the runner—because the localized heating at Position 1 is insufficient to reverse this trend in Fig. 2b. Because Δv and Δv act in opposite Z-directions, the total Z-displacement represents their net effect. In Fig. 2b and Fig. 3b, Δv produces a larger Z-displacement in the opposite direction to that induced by Δv ; the dominant out-of-plane Δv deformation is partially counteracted by the smaller, opposite contribution from Δv , yielding a total Z-displacement smaller than the Δv component alone. This behavior is consistent with Moldex3D’s warpage decomposition, in which different shrinkage modes may offset each other.
A concise explanation of this mechanism has been added to Supplementary Note 1.
Comment 12. Fig. 2c,d: Can the authors explain the reason to choose these voltage levels?
Response: The voltage levels shown in Fig. 2c,d were determined through the response surface methodology (RSM). In the face-centered central composite design (FCD), each of the eight heating-element groups was treated as an independent input variable. Because each element operates within a 0–24 V range, we selected three experimental levels—0, 12, and 24 V—with a uniform 12 V increment, consistent with standard FCD requirements (Supplementary Table 4). These levels were used only for constructing and fitting the RSM model.
After model development, the final voltage values used in Fig. 2c,d were obtained by applying a desirability-function optimization to the RSM equations (Eq. 1 for simulation and Eq. 2 for experiment) to achieve the target deformation profile. As we use a DC regulator capable of continuous control between 0–24 V, any optimized voltage value within this range can be practically implemented. Supplementary Table 11 lists these exact optimized voltages alongside the corresponding simulated and experimental deformation results.

Comment 17. Extended Data Fig. 2b: How did the authors ensure reproducibility of the measurement points across all the samples? How did they accurately mark the exact measurement point on these curved surfaces?
Response: As described in the Methods section, “A measurement frame was prepared by fixing three steel nails onto a glass slide with a leveling device and adhesive (Supplementary Fig. 4c). The impeller was placed with its parting surface facing upward. The blade root (1 mm thick) served as the reference plane.” Each impeller inherently contained a mold-defined datum feature at the blade root (near the runner root), allowing consistent positioning of all samples. The primary datum point (No. 0) was defined at the midpoint of the blade root (Supplementary Fig. 1a), providing a fixed reference for locating all subsequent measurement points.
To transfer measurement-point coordinates accurately onto the curved blade surfaces, we printed full-scale CAD drawings showing all measurement point locations. Benefiting from the thin and semi-transparent PP blade walls, each part was aligned directly over the drawing, enabling precise manual marking of the measurement points with a fine-tip marker. These marked points were then used for laser-distance measurements (see Supplementary Fig. 4b for examples). These procedures and clarifications have now been incorporated into the revised Methods section.
Although manual marking introduces some inevitable experimental variability, this was mitigated by robust replication. For each experimental condition, ten samples were molded, yielding ten measurements for each designated point. The mean value and its deviation, reported in Supplementary Fig. 4d (right), confirm the measurement consistency. To evaluate repeatability for displacement measurements, we conducted an ANOVA-based analysis. We have used preliminary data from 9 × 10 consecutive moulding cycles for a key sample geometry (the three-blade impeller), covering both regular IM (without localized thermal activation, No. 0) and 4D IM (with localized thermal activation, No. 1–8). Each experiment showed consistent deformation behaviour. Under identical IM conditions without localized heating, 10 parts were produced, and displacement was measured at 8 defined positions for each part. These 80 data points were used to quantify repeatability, summarized in Supplementary Table 4. The measurement system exhibits stable absolute repeatability across all positions, with a pooled standard deviation S = 0.0482. Similarly, the repeatability of 4D IM (localized thermal activation) was assessed by ANOVA. For each activation pattern (No. 1–8), 10 sequential parts were produced, giving 80 measurements per experiment. The resulting pooled standard deviations were 0.0199, 0.0135, 0.0185, 0.0109, 0.0168, 0.0179, 0.0268, and 0.0184, respectively, confirming good repeatability. Comment 21. Extended Data Fig. 6: Authors should scientifically explain the difference between: (b) fiber orientation and (c) random fiber orientation. Alos, why does (a) have a different scale factor?
Response: We have added the scientific explanations in Supplementary Note 3. Extended Data Fig. 6a (now Supplementary Fig. 13) presents the total Z-direction warpage displacement, whereas Figs. b–e show the individual effect displacements corresponding to specific mechanisms.
In Extended Data Fig. 6b (now Supplementary Fig. 13b), the bonded CGF-PA6 prepreg contains continuous glass fibers, whose orientations are defined in the simulation according to the prepreg’s weft and warp directions. These continuous fibers strongly restrict local shrinkage at the bonding region. As described in the Results section, this induces bending toward the bonding side (positive Z-direction). The weft-aligned prepreg produces significantly larger bending than the warp-aligned one, because the weft direction corresponds to the dominant fiber orientation and stiffness.
In Extended Data Fig. 6c (now Supplementary Fig. 13c), the SGF-PA6 base material contains short, randomly distributed glass fibers. Their orientation is primarily along the filling direction (X-direction), but the presence of the inserted CGF-PA6 prepreg disturbs the SGF orientation field. This results in different orientation-induced shrinkage patterns under the weft vs. warp configurations of the prepreg. Unlike the continuous-fiber case, the random SGF orientation effect drives bending toward the negative Z-direction, opposite to the CGF effect.
Fig. 6a uses a higher scale factor because the total Z-displacement is smaller than some of the individual effect displacements shown in Figs. 6b–e. A larger scale factor is therefore necessary to make the final warpage shape visually distinguishable from the component effect plots.

Comment 25. Supplementary Video 5: The gripping and un-gripping method/mechanism is not clear.
Response: The gripping/un-gripping mechanism of the 4D IM TPU hand-shaped parts relies on residual stress, nonuniform shrinkage, and gradient solidification during molding, which generate curling in the fingers. This provides a passive, reversible actuation mechanism without requiring external heating or pneumatic/electrical systems:
(1) Passive gripping (Curl-induced closure): Each TPU finger contains a curvature determined by the local thermal history, cooling gradients, and mold-part interactions during 4D IM. When assembled with a foldback clip (Supplementary Video 5), the pre-curled fingers face inward. Releasing the external clip force allows the intrinsic curling moment of the TPU fingers to close around an object, achieving a passive gripping state.
(2) Manual un-gripping (Elastic reopening): TPU’s high elasticity allows fingers to straighten when an external force is applied, either manually or via a simple mechanism. After the object is removed or the force is released, the stored elastic energy, combined with the curvature, returns the fingers to their curled shape.
This design creates a body-powered soft gripper: opening is externally initiated, while closing occurs autonomously via the programmed shape recovery. The gripping force is determined by the curvature and stiffness of each finger, allowing handling of objects with varying sizes and shapes. Different molded curvatures (Fig. 5c) yield variable gripping strengths and contact patterns.
We have added the Supplementary Note 4 to address this gripping and un-gripping method/mechanism.

The corresponding weft and warp orientations are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 12.” In Supplementary Fig. 12, we have also added arrows to clearly indicate the weft and warp directions of the continuous fiber orientations.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The paper presents an advanced 4D Injection Moulding (4D IM) platform capable of programmable deformations, selective in-mould bonding for multi-material and multi-functional structures, and integration of functional elements such as embedded magnets for soft robotics.
While the work demonstrates significant innovation, some improvements should be made to increase the final quality of the paper to be completely ready for submission.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for recognizing the "significant innovation" of our work and for providing constructive suggestions to enhance its impact.
Comment 1: A general remark: the Conclusion section is missing, together with Future works.
Response: We would like to note that the structure of our manuscript (Introduction → Results → Discussion → Methods) follows the standard formatting requirement for Nature Communications, as confirmed by the Editor. Therefore, we have maintained this structure. However, within this framework, we have added text about “Conclusion” and “Future works” in the Discussion section to summarize the key findings and contributions of the work as well as the future outlook.
Comment 2: More in detail, but also as a suggestion for Future works, there were areas where it was not possible to integrate more of the work done, with the purpose of moving the 4D IM platform from a laboratory-scale proof-of-concept toward a robust, industrially viable manufacturing technology: The feasibility of scaling the localised heating system and multi-point bonding for high-volume production remains unclear. The complexity and cost associated with multiple heating elements and precise voltage control may limit adoption in large-scale manufacturing.
Response: We fully agree that transitioning from laboratory demonstrations to an industrially viable process is a crucial next step. In the revised manuscript, we have expanded the Discussion to clearly address the scalability considerations of the localized heating system and multi-point bonding strategy. We have included a more detailed analysis of potential engineering routes for scaling and highlighted these as important directions for future development. “Localized thermal activation requires tooling with integrated heating elements, which increases mold complexity, energy consumption, and cost. Selective in-mold bonding currently relies on adhesive application, introducing potential variability in bond strength and surface finish, and bond displacement under high temperature and high-shear melt flow remains a critical challenge. Future developments of the 4D IM framework will target these limitations. One direction is the adoption of non-contact thermal activation methods (e.g., directed infrared heating60) to generate spatial T gradients without permanent mold modification, thereby improving flexibility, energy efficiency, and cost-effectiveness. Another is the exploration of alternative bonding strategies, such as temporary high-performance adhesives61 that form mechanical interlock interfaces between the bond part and cavity surface during molding and can be removed afterward to preserve surface quality.”
Comment 3: Although experimental correlations are generally strong, some parts, such as the caterpillar-shaped samples, show lower predictive accuracy (R² = 81.57%), indicating variability.
Response: We appreciate the Reviewer’s observation regarding the lower predictive accuracy for the caterpillar-shaped samples. We agree that this accuracy is lower than that obtained for the other geometries. The primary reason lies in the significantly higher geometric complexity of the caterpillar design: it contains five alternating thick sections, which introduce strong thickness-dependent shrinkage effects and more pronounced spatiotemporal gradients during solidification. These nonlinear effects interact sensitively with processing parameters, leading to greater variability and reduced predictability compared with the cross-shaped and hand-shaped parts whose geometry varies mainly within a single plane.
Comment 4: Data on repeated production cycles, mould wear, and long-term stability are currently lacking.
Response: Data on repeatability, mould wear, and long-term stability have now been partially addressed. Repeatability in injection moulding depends on part geometry, material, and the selected response parameter (e.g., mass, dimensions, or displacement). To evaluate repeatability for displacement measurements, we conducted an ANOVA-based analysis. We have added preliminary data from 9 × 10 consecutive moulding cycles for a key sample geometry (the three-blade impeller), covering both regular IM (without localized thermal activation, No. 0) and 4D IM (with localized thermal activation, No. 1–8). Each experiment showed consistent deformation behaviour. Under identical IM conditions without localized heating, 10 parts were produced, and displacement was measured at 8 defined positions for each part. These 80 data points were used to quantify repeatability, summarized in Supplementary Table 4. The measurement system exhibits stable absolute repeatability across all positions, with a pooled standard deviation S = 0.0482. Similarly, the repeatability of 4D IM (localized thermal activation) was assessed by ANOVA. For each activation pattern (No. 1–8), 10 sequential parts were produced, giving 80 measurements per experiment. The resulting pooled standard deviations were 0.0199, 0.0135, 0.0185, 0.0109, 0.0168, 0.0179, 0.0268, and 0.0184, respectively, confirming good repeatability. Details are provided in Supplementary Note 1.
We agree that mould wear, long-term machine stability, and durability across extended production cycles are important for industrial adoption. However, these factors depend strongly on equipment configuration and maintenance and are outside the scope of this initial technological study. Moreover, unlike conventional IM, the proposed 4D IM concept intentionally leverages controlled, localized thermal instability to produce diverse deformation outcomes from a single mould. A full durability evaluation—including mould longevity, machine cycling performance, material fatigue, and multi-cycle functional consistency—represents essential future work, which we have now noted explicitly in the Outlook section.
Comment 5: In TPU/Fe₃O₄ composites, particle aggregation at higher loadings reduces magnetic field uniformity, which may compromise actuation performance. Long-term mechanical behavior, including fatigue and multi-cycle performance, has not been fully investigated.
Response: We appreciate the Reviewer’s insights regarding particle aggregation and multi-cycle mechanical performance in TPU/Fe₃O₄ composites. We have expanded the discussion in the Method section: “Increasing Fe O content enhanced magnetic responsiveness but also induce particle aggregation, reducing magnetic field uniformity and increasing composite hardness and density. Consequently, actuation performance declined at the 4/6 TPU/Fe O ratio compared with the optimal 5/5 ratio.” We also now explicitly state that investigating long-term fatigue and cyclic performance of these composites is a key direction for future work in the Discussion section.
Comment 6: Demonstrations of soft robotic functionalities have been limited to controlled laboratory conditions. The performance under practical operating conditions, including higher loads, integration with industrial automation, and electronic systems, has not yet been validated.
Response: We appreciate the Reviewer’s comment regarding the validation of soft robotic functionalities under practical conditions. In this study, our demonstrations were performed in controlled laboratory settings to establish proof-of-concept and validate the actuation principles and programmable deformation of the 4D IM platform. We acknowledge that performance under higher loads, integration with industrial automation, and compatibility with electronic control systems remain to be investigated. Future work will focus on scaling these demonstrations to realistic operating environments, evaluating multi-cycle performance, mechanical robustness, and system integration, thereby bridging the gap between laboratory validation and industrial deployment.
Comment 7: The current studies provide limited insight into compliance with ISO or other industrial production and quality standards. Durability testing, functional certification, and standardization data are largely absent.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for highlighting the importance of standardization, industrial quality frameworks, and durability assessments. We agree that these aspects are essential for transitioning 4D IM from laboratory-scale demonstrations toward industrial adoption.
First, we would like to clarify that our study already references relevant ISO standards where applicable. For example, ISO 20457:2018 (“Plastics moulded parts — Tolerances and acceptance conditions”) is cited in the main text (Ref. 21) to contextualize the influence of shrinkage on dimensional tolerances and warpage in injection-molded parts. Since our work intentionally pursues the opposite direction—programmed deformation rather than its suppression—this standard does not directly apply as a performance benchmark for evaluating the outcomes of 4D IM.
Regarding measurement and testing, we agree that standardized methods are essential. While there is no dedicated ISO standard for deformation-displacement measurement in warped or shape-morphing IM parts, we employed a commercial non-contact laser displacement sensor (HG-C100), which avoids probe-induced elastic deformation inherent to contact methods. All measurements were analyzed using average, maximum, minimum, and standard deviation values to ensure statistical reliability.
All equipment used in this study—including the injection molding machine (Haitian ZE1200), infrared thermal imager (TUi260B), laser displacement sensor (HG-C100), torque blender (RM-200C), nanoindenter (G200), force gauge (SMF-20), optical microscope (CX40MRT), and Gauss meter (GS-25)—are standard commercial instruments. The polymers (PP 579S, TPU-6085F) were also commercial materials, and their physical properties were characterized using standard test methods such as ISO 1133, ISO 1183, and ASTM D792. These standardized data were subsequently used as material inputs in the Moldex3D simulations.
For the characterization of composite and elastomer parts, standardized mechanical tests were used wherever applicable. Specifically, bending tests on CGF/SGF-PA6 parts followed ISO 14125:1998, and nanoindentation experiments for CGF/SGF-PA6 and TPU/Fe₃O₄ samples were conducted according to ISO 14577 (now explicitly added in the Methods section). These provide standardized mechanical characterization data supporting the robustness of our conclusions.
The RSM modeling for programmable deformation followed established statistical standards, including full ANOVA, with reporting of F-values, p-values, Std. Dev. (standard deviation), coefficients of variation (C.V.), R2, adjusted R2, predicted R2, and Adequate Precision.
We acknowledge the Reviewer’s concern regarding durability and long-term functional performance. Functional demonstrations (such as soft robotic actuation) are more challenging to standardize due to the diversity of geometries, material combinations, and application-specific requirements. These functionalities are inherently performance-driven rather than governed by universal ISO norms.
Nevertheless, when 4D IM is translated to specific industrial applications, process- and product-specific standards can certainly be co-developed with industrial partners. Nonetheless, we have added key durability-related properties of the TPU material used—density (ASTM D792), tensile strength (ASTM D412), elongation at break (ASTM D412), tear strength (ASTM D624), and UV resistance (ISO 105-A02)—to the Methods section. These properties provide baseline insight into material reliability.
Durability of the full 4D IM system—including mold longevity, machine cycling, part fatigue, and multi-cycle functional performance—is indeed important but lies beyond the scope of this initial technological study. We have now explicitly stated in the Discussion that systematic durability evaluation, functional certification, and compliance with industrial standards will form an essential part of future work toward industrial deployment of 4D IM.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
Overall an interesting paper but the format must be standardized, 1.introduction, experimental method, 3. results 4. conclusion etc. A thorough review of the wording within the text also needs to done.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for their positive assessment of our paper as “interesting.” Regarding the manuscript structure, we would like to clarify that our current format (Introduction → Results → Discussion → Methods) follows the required structure for Nature Communications, as also confirmed by the Editor. Accordingly, we have maintained this organization. However, we have thoroughly revised the manuscript to enhance coherence and logical flow, as also suggested by Reviewer #1. In addition, we have conducted a comprehensive line-by-line edit to improve clarity, consistency, and wording throughout. We believe these revisions have substantially strengthened the manuscript, and we hope it is now suitable for publication in Nature Communications.
